📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How Codex runs commands on your machine with limits you control.
  • Industry observers note that at OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a upcoming window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents.
  • A ⁠(opens in a upcoming window)sandbox⁠(opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How Codex runs commands on your machine with limits you control.

By Michael Bolin, Member of Technical Staff.

Industry observers note that at OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a upcoming window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex⁠(opens in a new window), to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control.

A ⁠(opens in a upcoming window)sandbox⁠(opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs. For a photo-organizing task, you might configure the Codex sandbox to let commands read and modify files in ~/Pictures while blocking network access to prevent uploads. For code review, you might allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. Users configure the Codex sandbox through ⁠(opens in a new window)permission profiles⁠(opens in a new window), which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session.

It has been revealed that in this article, we’ll start with the tradeoffs behind Codex’s sandbox defaults, then explain the sandbox’s design and how the harness uses it to run commands. We’ll show how end owners and enterprises can tailor its permissions to their needs and how developers can reuse the sandbox in their own tools. Finally, we’ll examine how these restrictions are enforced on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

In Codex, our philosophy is to specify conservative defaults for the sandbox that still enable meaningful work. For example, with a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace permission profile:.

Allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only. This lets Codex edit source code without seeking permission for every change, while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks.

According to recent reports, allows broad filesystem reads, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions. Compilers, runtimes, and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries, and configuration outside the repository. Restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere on the machine may also remain readable (such as config files containing API keys).

Disables network access. This blocks direct uploads to external services, including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read. It also prevents legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies, which require additional access.

These restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior, but harmful actions are still possible. For example, the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier. Such a change might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git. If the user’s editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox. This is why we take a defense in depth approach: the sandbox limits what commands can access, while training and alignment help the model use that access in accordance with the user’s intent.

For guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment, see the Codex security cookbook⁠(opens in a new window).

Virtual machines and containers⁠(opens in a fresh window) are two popular mechanisms used for sandboxing, but we take a different approach with the Codex sandbox. Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

For example, consider using Codex to develop an iOS app on a Mac. If you decided to sandbox Codex by running it inside Docker, Codex would not be able to run the iOS build toolchain composed of native Mac executables, nor could it launch the iPhone simulator to run the code. A Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host, but those operations would execute outside the container’s sandbox and would need their own restrictions. For Codex, we prefer to keep things simple by investing heavily in OS-specific sandboxing so Codex can run in the environment that is most appropriate to the task at hand.

Sources indicate that the harness exposes these OS-specific sandboxing mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows, and Linux. This API takes a command and a permission profile. If the permission profile allows limited network access, the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits:.

It has been revealed that this function starts the process in a sandbox and returns a Child handle the harness can use to wait for it to finish. Each child process inherits its parent’s sandbox constraints, so those restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

Recent findings suggest that the following diagram demonstrates how these pieces fit together, from configuration to running a sandboxed command. The sections that follow explain each stage.

As explained in Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop, the Codex harness is responsible for executing tool calls generated by the model. For coding tasks, the most commonly used tool is a shell tool, which runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. Here we’ll examine the one-shot ⁠(opens in a fresh window)exec_command⁠(opens in a new window) shell tool⁠(opens in a new window) to illustrate how the harness employs the sandbox to achieve the desired protections.This is a simplified version of how the exec_command tool call would be honored by the Codex harness without sandboxing:.

In a recent development, to sandbox the command, the harness replaces the call to subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(). The harness supplies the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy:.

The exec_command tool also lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, but the harness decides whether to grant the request:.

In a recent development, when use_default is specified, the harness uses the default sandbox config for the turn. with_additional_permissions requests expanded access within the sandbox, while require_escalated requests execution outside it. The harness evaluates the request based on the user’s preferences before executing the command. (For example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window).) If execution is authorized, Codex will pass the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy to perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing() with the command arguments from the original ExecCommandToolCall.

The shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files. This reuse extends beyond the harness: the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools, as we’ll see later. Next, we’ll look at how permission profiles are defined.

Recent findings suggest that A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects. You can define your own profiles under [permissions] in config.toml. For example, the following defines a profile named dev that extends⁠(opens in a new window) the built-in :workspace profile:.

The dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace. Filesystem entries can grant read-only access (read), grant read and write access (write), or block access entirely (deny).

The :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project’s workspace roots. By default, the Codex CLI uses its working directory as its sole workspace root, while the ChatGPT desktop app uses the project’s source folders. Codex applies each rule to every root, so the .vscode entry in dev makes the .vscode directory read-only under each root.

In addition to its own rules, dev inherits the following protections from :workspace:.

When it comes to configuring the network for the sandbox in Codex, there are roughly three options:.

Disable all network access (default for the :workspace profile).

Enable full, direct network access (default for the :danger-full-access profile).

Restrict network access to a proxy, which decides what to let through based on the permission profile.

To give dev direct network access, set permissions.dev.network.enabled = true at the top level of config.toml. This grants full network access when the network proxy is disabled.

To restrict dev to a set of domains, enable the network proxy and configure its domain rules:.

Domain rules support exact names and wildcard patterns, with explicit deny rules taking precedence over allow rules. Requests to other domains require approval or are blocked, as described in Network proxy below.

Industry observers note that individual consumers can configure defaults that apply across projects and override them for a particular trusted project. Enterprise administrators may also want to configure defaults for their users and constrain which settings those users can change. Codex supports both through layered configuration and managed requirements.

According to recent reports, as described in Configuration precedence,⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) Codex merges settings from multiple config.toml files. Tables are merged recursively, with the higher-precedence source winning when values conflict. Arrays are replaced as a whole.

Industry observers note that this is why permission profiles use tables for filesystem paths and network domains. A team can add or override individual entries in its own configuration and automatically inherit changes to all other entries in the organization’s base configuration:.

Recent findings suggest that administrators can also supply managed requirements⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) through requirements.toml to constrain owners’ configuration choices. These requirements can come from multiple sources, including system files and cloud-provided policy. A common use case is to specify allowed_permission_profiles to constrain the set of permission profiles an enterprise user can select. For example, an administrator could specify these cloud requirements:.

The cloud requirements would take precedence over the system requirements file at /etc/codex/requirements.toml, so an entry in that file cannot override the explicit ":danger-full-access" = false above. Leaving :workspace unspecified allows another requirements layer to supply that entry. Profiles whose entries are false or absent from the final merged table are unavailable.This separation lets organizations enforce limits while users tailor their configuration within those limits. The resulting permission profiles can be used by the harness or applied directly to a command, as we’ll see next.

The Codex CLI provides a sandbox command to facilitate running an arbitrary command under a permission profile defined in the Codex config. This is commonly used to test out the profile, ensuring that the sandbox prevents the behavior it was designed to block.

It has been revealed that for example, the following command attempts to configure VS Code to run a malicious auto-formatter on save. Assuming .vscode already exists, the dev profile defined above should block this write because that directory is read-only (codex sandbox treats cwd as a workspace root by default):.

Indeed, on macOS this fails with:.

The codex sandbox command makes Codex’s sandboxing mechanism available independently of an agent session. You can use the same configuration language and platform-specific enforcement to constrain commands launched by your own tools.

According to recent reports, for a stdio MCP server configured in config.toml, the Codex harness does not attempt to sandbox the command used to start the server. Codex cannot reliably infer which files or network services that server needs, so applying a default sandbox profile could break an otherwise valid configuration.

For example, the standard way to configure the @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory⁠(opens in a new window) MCP server for use with Codex is as follows:.

Because this npx command runs unsandboxed, it can write files and make network requests with the same permissions as the user running Codex, which is overly permissive. To lock it down, we can define a permission profile named memory-mcp and then wrap the original npx command with codex sandbox --permission-profile memory-mcp to limit where the server can write and to prevent it from accessing the network:.

Recent findings suggest that before starting the server, create its data directory and populate the npm cache with the pinned package. That lets npx --offline launch the server under a profile that disables network access:.

Once the package is cached, Codex can start the memory server without network access, with writes limited to the npm cache and the server’s data directory.

The sandbox implementation turns a permission profile into restrictions enforced by the operating system. The network proxy’s core request-handling and policy logic is shared across all three major operating systems, while proxy setup and integration with the sandbox are OS-specific. We’ll examine the shared proxy first, followed by the implementations for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

To enforce a permission profile’s network restrictions, the harness starts a network proxy and configures the sandbox to allow connections to it while blocking direct connections to external hosts. The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

In a recent development, in the Codex repo, the network proxy is implemented in the codex-network-proxy⁠(opens in a new window) crate, which the harness uses as a library, though it can also be built as a standalone CLI⁠(opens in a new window). When enabled, codex-network-proxy starts both an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy by default. These proxy addresses are communicated to the process spawned by the sandbox via environment variables. In addition to injecting standard environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY, a number of well-known application-specific environment variables⁠(opens in a new window) (such as PIP_PROXY) are injected, as well. Admittedly, not all programs honor these environment variables. If a program attempts a direct connection to an external host, the operating system’s sandbox restrictions block it, as described in the platform-specific sections below.

Sources indicate that the network proxy is responsible for implementing the network restrictions defined in a permission profile. For example, the dev profile shown earlier allows requests to *.openai.com and explicitly denies requests to evil.example. When a request targets a domain that does not match an allow or deny rule, the proxy can suspend the request while it delegates to the harness for approval. Like the shell command example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window). Upon receiving a decision, the proxy either allows the request to proceed or rejects it with an error response.

Sources indicate that the order matters here because even a DNS lookup can leak information encoded in a hostname. The proxy therefore resolves the requested hostname only after determining that it is allowed or approved. Note that broad wildcard rules or access to DNS services can still permit DNS-based exfiltration.

Recent findings suggest that on macOS, Codex uses Seatbelt⁠(opens in a upcoming window), Apple’s kernel-enforced sandboxing mechanism. Seatbelt policies are written in Sandbox Profile Language (SBPL), a Scheme-based language for expressing sandbox restrictions. Codex invokes Seatbelt through macOS’s /usr/bin/sandbox-exec command. Like codex sandbox, it takes options describing the sandbox followed by the command to run:.

Recent findings suggest that the PROFILE is a string of SBPL that contains entries that configure the sandbox. For example, the following SBPL snippet makes /dev/null and /dev/zero readable and writable under the sandbox policy:.

When the network proxy is enabled as part of a sandbox invocation, rules like the following are injected into the profile to limit connections to the appropriate local ports:.

Codex’s base profile starts with (deny default), so outbound connections remain blocked unless explicitly allowed.

Finally, the SBPL can contain placeholders using (param):.

which are populated by the -Dkey=value options passed to sandbox-exec.

To implement its own sandbox API, Codex builds up the list of arguments⁠(opens in a new window) to sandbox-exec starting from a base policy⁠(opens in a new window), and then uses permission_profile and other context to amend it to produce the complete Seatbelt profile. The resulting profile and accompanying -D arguments configure the restrictions enforced by Seatbelt, while the network proxy enforces additional network rules. With the full arg list assembled, the invocation of sandbox-exec is straightforward.

Generating the correct SBPL is challenging because Apple does not document the language for third-party use. Indeed, man sandbox-exec states The sandbox-exec command is DEPRECATED (as is the sandbox_init() library function documented via man 3 sandbox_init). Despite the deprecation warning, macOS still ships Seatbelt profiles in /usr/share/sandbox, and third-party software, including Google Chrome and Chromium⁠(opens in a new window), continues to rely on Seatbelt. As such, we plan to continue to use Seatbelt for the foreseeable future.

To create the sandbox on Linux, Codex uses a combination of bubblewrap⁠(opens in a new window) (bwrap), a command-line tool for constructing isolated environments, and seccomp-bpf⁠(opens in a new window), a Linux kernel mechanism for filtering system calls. An internal helper named codex-linux-sandbox coordinates the setup. Like sandbox-exec on macOS, it takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run:.

When filesystem isolation or proxy routing is required, codex-linux-sandbox invokes bwrap to create the initial sandbox environment. bwrap then introduces codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec inside it. This second invocation uses seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions before running the user’s command.

According to recent reports, to construct that initial sandbox environment, Codex uses bubblewrap to create a filesystem view in a separate mount namespace that reflects the permission profile’s filesystem rules. Because this is fundamental to the sandbox implementation, Codex vendors its own copy of bwrap in case the user has not installed their own, but it prefers a compatible installation of ⁠(opens in a new window)bwrap⁠(opens in a new window) found on PATH, when available. Empirically, some Linux distributions disable access to user namespaces by default⁠(opens in a new window), but grant an exception for the system bwrap.

Sources indicate that also like sandbox-exec, bwrap takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run within the sandbox. Instead of using a custom config language like SBPL, bwrap uses individual flags for configuration. Codex uses the following options to create the filesystem view:.

--bind to specify a writable file or directory.

--ro-bind to specify a read-only file or directory.

--perms 000 --tmpfs DIR --remount-ro DIR to deny access to DIR.

--perms 000 --ro-bind-data FD FILE to deny access to FILE (where FD is an open file descriptor to /dev/null).

To apply deny globs using these options, Codex expands them to concrete paths before launching each command. Upcoming matching paths are not automatically added to that command’s sandbox restrictions.

Codex also specifies options such as --unshare-ipc and --unshare-pid to prevent the sandbox from accessing other types of resources on the host, so bubblewrap affects more than just file visibility.

Recent findings suggest that when using bubblewrap, Codex passes --unshare-net whenever networking is disabled or connections must go through the network proxy, which will create a latest network namespace for the sandbox. We then use seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions on the networking system calls and socket families available to the command.

It has been revealed that specifically, we use the seccompiler crate⁠(opens in a new window) to dynamically compile a BPF program based on the desired filters⁠(opens in a new window) and apply it to a launcher process in the sandbox so the constraints are inherited by the entire process tree. As such, bwrap does not run the user’s command, but runs the codex-linux-sandbox launcher with its own config args followed by the user’s command:.

To apply seccomp filters without elevated privileges, the launcher sets Linux’s no_new_privs flag⁠(opens in a new window). This flag is inherited by child processes and prevents them from gaining additional privileges when executing another program, such as a setuid executable.

Recent findings suggest that the seccomp filters depend on the network configuration. When network access is disabled, we block a number of network-related syscalls, such as connect(2) and bind(2). Though when the network proxy is enabled in the sandbox, we allow IP sockets so the TCP listener created by codex-linux-sandbox can be reached, but block the creation of standalone Unix domain sockets by default, as those could enable inadvertent access to resources from the host.

According to recent reports, when the sandbox configuration merits the use of the network proxy, the Codex harness creates one instance of the proxy that can be reused across multiple invocations of codex-linux-sandbox within the same Codex thread. Each sandbox needs a way to reach that shared proxy from its isolated network namespace. Codex provides a loopback TCP listener inside that namespace and arranges for a process outside the sandbox to accept its connections and relay them to the proxy.

The following diagrams illustrate this setup for one proxy endpoint, with one connection through it shown in the final diagram. Before launching bubblewrap, codex-linux-sandbox creates a Unix socket pair to serve as a control channel and forks itself. The child runs run_host_bridge() and waits to receive the listener’s file descriptor over that channel:.

In this example, the parent process uses exec to replace its program image with bwrap. This sets up the sandbox and releases codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec within it, passing along the FD for the control channel:.

Inside the sandbox’s network namespace, the second invocation of codex-linux-sandbox creates a loopback TCP listener and passes its file descriptor via the socket. The listener remains associated with the sandbox’s network namespace, allowing the child process that remained outside the sandbox to accept connections from sandboxed programs while opening its upstream connections in the host’s network namespace. After the handoff, both processes close their control-channel descriptors, and the process inside the sandbox closes its copy of the listener.

Industry observers note that once the TCP listener is ready, the process inside the sandbox sets the appropriate value for HTTP_PROXY⁠(opens in a new window) and related environment variables to point to that listener. It then applies seccomp before forking and executing the user’s command:.

According to recent reports, the process outside the sandbox keeps the listener open. For each accepted connection, it opens a connection to the configured proxy and relays data in both directions.This additional machinery gives the command its own network namespace, including a separate loopback interface. On macOS, Seatbelt allows the command to connect directly to specified ports on the host’s loopback interface. On Linux, the command instead connects to a listener inside its isolated namespace, and a process outside the sandbox relays those connections to the configured proxy. The descriptor handoff makes this connection possible without exposing the host’s network namespace to the command.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, we implemented and wrote about our sandboxing efforts on Windows. Since then, Microsoft has released a library called MXC alongside new features for process isolation inside the Windows operating system. We are at the moment replacing our existing sandbox with one that makes use of the MXC library.

In a recent development, MXC (Microsoft eXecution Container) is a sandboxed code execution system⁠(opens in a new window) from Microsoft that supports several containment backends across Windows, Linux, and macOS. Codex supports an MXC-based sandbox on compatible Windows devices, using native process isolation to restrict commands within the user’s existing environment.

We are transitioning to MXC to improve security and usability while addressing several limitations of our existing Windows sandbox:.

Need for elevated/admin access to set up the sandbox.

Expensive/slow ACL checking and setting operations.

Persistent sandbox setup state on the host machine, including.

Recent findings suggest that MXC exposes a JSON configuration schema⁠(opens in a latest window). Codex uses the MXC SDK⁠(opens in a new window) to construct an execution request following that schema and containing the command, working directory, environment, and permissions. Those permissions cover filesystem and network access, along with Windows resources such as the desktop and clipboard.

Codex uses fixed settings for several controls to balance compatibility and security. It permits registry reads and retains the Win32k and desktop access PowerShell needs during startup. Clipboard access, input injection, and desktop and system-settings controls are disabled. Finally, MXC is prevented from falling back to modifying host filesystem permissions.

Codex translates the permission profile’s filesystem and network rules into MXC’s configuration. Using the earlier dev profile, and assuming:.

C:\, D:\ and Z:\ are the machine’s only local drives.

The workspace root and working directory are C:\work\demo.

The user’s home directory is D:\Customers\dev, so ~/build-cache resolves to D:\Users\dev\build-cache.

The deny glob matches only C:\work\demo\config\dev.env and C:\work\demo\config\prod.env.

The corresponding MXC settings would include:.

MXC’s filesystem policy denies access by default. Codex therefore adds read-only grants for the local drive roots to provide the broad reads allowed by this profile. These grants apply recursively, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions.

One wrinkle: writable drive-root grants do not apply recursively, so Codex expands them to include the drive’s existing immediate children.

More-specific paths override ancestor grants, so C:\work\demo can be writable beneath a read-only C:\, while C:\work\demo\.git remains read-only.

When different path spellings or symlink/junction aliases refer to the same path, MXC applies the stricter permission: deny takes precedence over read-only, which takes precedence over read-write.

MXC takes concrete deny paths only, so Codex expands deny globs to matching files and directories before launch. New paths that match the glob are not automatically added while the command is running.

Recent findings suggest that domain rules such as *.openai.com are enforced by the shared Codex network proxy described earlier. Codex runs that proxy outside the sandbox and passes its addresses to the command through the same standard *_PROXY environment variables as mentioned previously. MXC blocks direct external connections while allowing host-loopback connections, including access to the proxy. Other local services remain reachable.

In a recent development, across macOS, Linux, and Windows, the harness uses the same sandbox API to launch commands under a permission profile. The platform-specific implementations handle the setup needed to apply those restrictions.

Industry observers note that writing and executing code gives agents a flexible way to solve problems beyond software development. The Codex sandbox lets them use that capability in the user’s existing environment with explicit limits on filesystem and network access. It is a reusable primitive within the harness, and the codex sandbox command makes it available to tools you build yourself.

Sources indicate that as agents take on more tasks, we want to make sandboxing practical for more tools and environments. That means making permissions easier to configure and taking advantage of better operating system protections as they become available. Our goal is to expand what agents can do while keeping people in control of what they can access.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that amazon Cognito now supports OAuth client ID metadata documents (CIMD).
  • In a recent development, with CIMD, a client uses an HTTPS URL as its client ID and publishes a JSON metadata document at that URL.
  • Industry observers note that CIMD is available on the Essentials and Plus feature aims in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available.

It has been revealed that amazon Cognito now supports OAuth client ID metadata documents (CIMD). Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for consumers, AI agents, and microservices in minutes. With CIMD, Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients and AI agents can sign users in to your user pool without registering a separate app client. Previously, each external client needed its own app client, either created in advance or through dynamic client registration, and you had to manage and clean up those clients over time.

In a recent development, with CIMD, a client uses an HTTPS URL as its client ID and publishes a JSON metadata document at that URL. When the client starts sign-in, Cognito fetches and validates the document and uses it to identify the client and validate its sign-in request. You decide which clients to accept with CIMD policies that map URL patterns to one of your app clients, and Cognito grants only the scopes and grant types that both the app client and the metadata document allow. For example, a tech giant that runs an MCP server can accept an AI assistant by allowing the URL where that assistant publishes its metadata without creating or maintaining an app client for it.

Industry observers note that CIMD is available on the Essentials and Plus feature aims in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see Client ID metadata documents (CIMD) in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

#16703. Industry News: AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2029 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • Industry observers note that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • Sources indicate that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

Industry observers note that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many upcoming tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

Sources indicate that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates upcoming tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

Industry observers note that A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

Industry observers note that the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

Sources indicate that the user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Sources indicate that feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little upcoming training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

According to recent reports, the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

According to recent reports, these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Recent findings suggest that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

Sources indicate that autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into upcoming executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

According to recent reports, autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

According to recent reports, identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates upcoming tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

According to recent reports, together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

Industry observers note that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Recent findings suggest that failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

According to recent reports, A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Industry observers note that passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

Sources indicate that A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

It has been revealed that the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We plan to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

Recent findings suggest that we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

Industry observers note that autoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

Sources indicate that the synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

In a recent development, we also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

Industry observers note that the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates upcoming tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

#16697. The Agent Stated It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

The Agent Stated It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • According to recent reports, A customer writes in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

According to recent reports, A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

Industry observers note that the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Sources indicate that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

Sources indicate that an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

It has been revealed that you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

In a recent development, final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

In a recent development, A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

Sources indicate that an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

According to recent reports, we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Recent findings suggest that starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

In a recent development, table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

Industry observers note that one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Sources indicate that only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Industry observers note that kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Industry observers note that claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Sources indicate that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

According to recent reports, A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

Recent findings suggest that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Sources indicate that cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Sources indicate that table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

Recent findings suggest that what to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

Industry observers note that at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Recent findings suggest that gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Industry observers note that now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

According to recent reports, the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

#16695. Industry News: Research acceleration: The jagged frontier
