📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one.
  • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
  • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something fresh, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

Sources indicate that FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

It has been revealed that for edits, each region states where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

In a recent development, everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

It has been revealed that FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

In a recent development, A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

Industry observers note that so one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

It has been revealed that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

It has been revealed that in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

According to recent reports, each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In a recent development, in FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

Recent findings suggest that the noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

It has been revealed that the distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Industry observers note that attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:.

In a recent development, the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are newly introduced to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

According to recent reports, get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

Latest Update: Introducing ambient networking for GKE

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment.
  • The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.
  • The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In a recent development, network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment. Today, we are announcing the general availability of ambient networking for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This milestone marks an notable evolution in how your run service mesh on GKE, bringing a sidecar-less architecture into production. Introduced earlier this year, ambient networking decouples functionality traditionally provided as a service mesh from application workloads, allowing platform operators and developers to help secure, observe, and route traffic without the resource overhead and operational complexity of managing sidecar proxies.

The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.

The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.

At the same time, several Node-level management components operate securely within the gke-managed-ambient namespace:.

Ambient networking runtime interface (NRI) plugin: Integrates with the NRI to perform low-level network redirection, intercepting traffic to and from ambient-enabled application pods.

xDS agent (ambient agent): Runs inside the node proxy pod to receive xDS configuration updates from Traffic Director and request certificates from the GKE control plane on-demand.

Node proxy (L4 Envoy proxy): A high-performance, shared per-node Envoy instance that processes intercepted L4 traffic, enforces mutual TLS (mTLS), evaluates authorization policies, performs load balancing, and emits rich telemetry metrics.

Service pods: The user’s application/service pods communicate through the GKE node proxy to perform service to service mTLS across the cluster.

Together, these features combine to deliver a number of advanced capabilities for GKE environments:.

Zero Trust architecture: Ambient networking allows customers to establish a Zero Trust security posture. Traffic between workloads can be automatically encrypted using mutual TLS (mTLS) with managed workload identities, helping protect and secure service-to-service communication across the cluster.

Ambient networking delivers tangible value for GKE operators:.

Simpler operations: Traditionally, service mesh products rely on injecting sidecar containers directly into every workload pod. Ambient networking removes this sidecar dependency by shifting networking features to shared node components. This fully managed solution simplifies deployment and streamlines day-to-day cluster operations.

Simplified lifecycle management: When proxy logic is decoupled from application containers, lifecycle management is simplified. Upgrading proxy versions or applying configuration updates helps avoid restarting application workloads or scheduling downtime windows, enabling continuous availability for your services. Ambient networking can reduce administrative overhead and application disruption an average of four times annually by eliminating pod restarts required by CVE patches for L4 mesh usage.This fully managed solution can be installed either at cluster creation time or added to an existing cluster. Ongoing maintenance to the cluster components is handled by automated systems and is performed along with normal GKE cluster maintenance.

According to recent reports, simplifying adoption by removing the cost and complexity barriers of sidecars. Try it out in your GKE environment and experience the benefits of ambient networking:.

fully managed installation and upgrades.

service-to-service mTLS and authorization policies.

lower resource usage than sidecars.

See our documentation for more information: https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ambient-overview.

Pricing: https://cloud.google.com/products/gke-service-networking/pricing.

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

According to recent reports, meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that looks, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Sources indicate that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

Recent findings suggest that the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Industry observers note that grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Sources indicate that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

Sources indicate that the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

According to recent reports, video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

It has been revealed that the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Recent findings suggest that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

According to recent reports, now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

Sources indicate that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

Industry observers note that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

Recent findings suggest that we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

Industry observers note that we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

It has been revealed that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Industry observers note that AWS Device Farm, a service for testing mobile and web apps, now provides Test Insights for Appium, Espresso, and XCUITest runs across multiple devices. Test Insights helps you and AI agents understand the health of your tests and resolve failures faster by providing a detailed breakdown of your test suite by device and by test.

With Test Insights, Device Farm's existing APIs now return enhanced test metadata, failure root cause with stack trace, a video for each test, start and stop times, median and average times spent on each device and test, and test counts by result. With this data in one place, your agents spend less time and fewer tokens looking for the root cause of test failures, and the AWS Device Farm troubleshooting skill uses it to help diagnose failed runs and suggest fixes. Test Insights is available alongside any default and custom test reports you generate, at no additional cost.

Test Insights is included in all AWS Regions where Device Farm is available.

To get started, see Test Insights in the AWS Device Farm Developer Guide.

Latest Update: Amazon Route 53 now offers Advanced Hosted Zones

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (292 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that amazon Route 53 now offers Advanced Hosted Zones, a new hosted zone tier with additional guardrails, visibility, and resilience features.
  • In a recent development, A single mistaken DNS change can take part of your domain offline, such as deleting a record that is still serving traffic or removing a delegation that resolvers are still using.
  • To get started, create a fresh Advanced Hosted Zone or upgrade an existing hosted zone, then turn on the guardrails you want.

Industry observers note that amazon Route 53 now offers Advanced Hosted Zones, a new hosted zone tier with additional guardrails, visibility, and resilience features. Advanced Hosted Zones include Change Guardrails that prevent accidental record deletions, record-level Change History, and public DNS fallback in private hosted zones.

In a recent development, A single mistaken DNS change can take part of your domain offline, such as deleting a record that is still serving traffic or removing a delegation that resolvers are still using. To protect against this, customers build their own validation pipelines, review processes, and audit tooling. With Change Guardrails turned on, Route 53 checks each change before applying it. It blocks deleting a record that is still receiving DNS queries, a record that an alias record in the same hosted zone points to, or a delegation that is still in use. When a guardrail blocks a change, Route 53 rejects the whole request with an error that explains why, and no records change. Guardrails apply to every change, including changes from infrastructure as code tools. Change History gives you a record-level history of changes to your hosted zone, retained for 365 days, so you can see what changed and when.

To get started, create a fresh Advanced Hosted Zone or upgrade an existing hosted zone, then turn on the guardrails you want. You can use the Route 53 console, API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. Advanced Hosted Zones are priced separately from Standard Hosted Zones. For rates, see the Route 53 pricing page.

Advanced Hosted Zones are available in all AWS commercial Regions where Route 53 public and private hosted zones are available. To learn more, see Advanced Hosted Zones in the Route 53 Developer Guide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

It has been revealed that overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

It has been revealed that alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

In a recent development, the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

It has been revealed that while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the latest release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

Industry observers note that we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 reveals strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

According to recent reports, the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Industry observers note that structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

It has been revealed that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Recent findings suggest that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Sources indicate that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Sources indicate that project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

Breaking: How Vodafone is using the Data Engineering Agent to improve their data pipelines

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manager, Data & Analytics Engineering, Vodafone.
  • It has been revealed that for large organizations, building and maintaining data pipelines is one of the most complex tasks that data engineering teams are tasked with.
  • In this blog post, Vodafone Czech Republic describes how it has used the Data Engineering Agent to modernize and optimize BigQuery stored procedures, transforming them into modern data pipelines and reducing pipeline execution times by half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sr. Manager, Data & Analytics Engineering, Vodafone.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

It has been revealed that for large organizations, building and maintaining data pipelines is one of the most complex tasks that data engineering teams are tasked with. In BigQuery environments, the Data Engineering Agent can help, leveraging Gemini to to automate these workflows.

In this blog post, Vodafone Czech Republic describes how it has used the Data Engineering Agent to modernize and optimize BigQuery stored procedures, transforming them into modern data pipelines and reducing pipeline execution times by half. - Pedro Esteves, Google Cloud.

The Data Engineering Agent makes it easy to build and maintain modern data pipelines. The agent is available in BigQuery pipelines and Dataform. At Vodafone, we used the agent directly in Dataform to build Dataform pipelines. As shown in the example below, the Data Engineering Agent takes natural language instructions together with any code provided in the instruction file to build the Dataform pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that vodafone Czech Republic uses many BigQuery stored procedures to transform data for business purposes. These stored procedures are a legacy of a previous on-premises data warehouse migration to BigQuery. Many of them contain 2,000 or 3,000 lines of code and run sequentially.

Compared to a modular Dataform approach created by the Data Engineering Agent, there are several known disadvantages of maintaining legacy, multi-thousand-line stored procedures, as described in the table below.

Legacy stored procedures (Monolith).

Single file, 1000s of lines, complex logic mixed.

Copy/Paste code blocks (prone to drift).

functions and ref() for strict logic reuse.

Automated testing (Unique, Not Null, Referential Integrity) built-in.

Comments in code (usually outdated).

Auto-generated documentation with lineage graph.

Manual scheduling; hard-coded dependency management.

Automatic execution based on lineage (DAG).

To solve the problems of running and maintaining legacy stored procedures, we used the Data Engineering Agent to migrate some of the stored procedures into Dataform pipelines.

The Data Engineering Agent was able to parallelize the code into independent steps which are then run in parallel to improve readability and performance. See the example below:.

The Data Engineering Agent can understand dependencies between the tables and cache certain intermediate tables using BigQuery materialized views. This means that tables that are used in downstream processes can be cached, speeding up code execution and reducing cost.

Having a modular pipeline allows us to facilitate end-to-end orchestration and pipeline dependencies to meet our SLAs. Before using Dataform, we had to manually control pipeline execution by creating metadata tables with several checkpoints and logs. Dependencies between stored procedures jobs were also maintained manually in a spreadsheet. By executing the pipeline in Dataform, all the dependencies and execution logs are handled by Dataform.

Sources indicate that because the code is now split into several steps, it’s possible to execute only a subset of the actions in Dataform rather than running the entire stored procedure. This can help with debugging and gives us the flexibility to only run the relevant sections of the code.

Industry observers note that there’s a trade-off between parallelization and caching. When we prompted the Data Engineering Agent to parallelize our procedures, we noticed an increase in cost.

When running a standard sequential stored procedure, BigQuery caches the base table for the first thread. However, splitting this logic into parallel streams can inadvertently negate those caching benefits, causing full table scans for each thread.

To solve this, we asked the Data Engineering Agent to create materialized views for intermediate tables. These views effectively pre-cache the data, ensuring that your parallelized queries remain performant and cost-efficient.

To make the agent parallelize the code more efficiently we gave it specific instructions on which areas (staging tables) we were interested in parallelizing.

Sources indicate that deploying Data Engineering Agent delivered immediate and measurable impact, specifically in addressing the toil associated with legacy migrations. The agent successfully achieved high-fidelity replication of all stored procedures, ensuring 1:1 logic parity with minimal human intervention.

Industry observers note that by automating the conversion of complex ETL pipelines, the agent achieved a 90% reduction in migration time compared with traditional manual approaches. What would have typically required weeks of engineering effort was completed in a fraction of the time, freeing engineers to focus on other key tasks.

Recent findings suggest that furthermore, the modernization of the underlying infrastructure resulted in substantial performance gains. Post-migration benchmarks indicate that the new data pipelines run twice as fast, significantly reducing query latency and increasing overall data throughput.

And as we previously discussed, instructing the agent to cache intermediate tables led to a 30% reduction in costs.

Recent findings suggest that beyond accelerating development and reducing costs, these agentic tools are also changing the way data engineers approach their work. Rather than spending significant time on repetitive migration and optimization tasks, engineers can collaborate with agents to explore different implementation options, validate design decisions, and accelerate delivery. This shift is encouraging teams to adopt new ways of working, where agentic capabilities become an integral part of the development process and help shape how data solutions are designed, delivered, and maintained.

At Vodafone, we’re planning to scale the use of the Data Engineering Agent across the company in the following key areas:.

Standardized Dataform template repository: Establishing a central repository for Dataform templates allows for consistent architecture and design patterns across different projects and teams, helping ensure quality and alignment with global standards.

Global market onboarding: We will expand the Data Engineering Agent deployment across key Vodafone markets including the Czech Republic (CZ), Romania (RO), Ireland (IE), Germany (DE), and the United Kingdom (UK), to drive widespread adoption and modernization.

Integration with developer environments (IDEs): Deepening the integration of agentic capabilities directly into developer workflows (such as VS Code, and and Antigravity) will enable engineers to leverage Data Engineering Agent features within their existing tools and IDEs.

Federated CI/CD governance: Implementing a centralized yet flexible governance framework for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) will allow individual markets to maintain autonomy while adhering to corporate quality and security policies.

Modernization of legacy stored procedures at scale: By systematically migrating complex, legacy workloads — specifically SAS code, BTEQ scripts, and MicroStrategy — into modern Dataform pipelines will allow us to reduce technical debt and accelerate transformation across the enterprise.

To learn more about transforming your enterprise data architecture for the agentic era, download our complete Data Agents Guidebook or explore Google Cloud’s Rapid Migration and Modernization Program (RaMP). To get started building and optimizing your own data pipelines with the agent today, visit the Data Engineering Agent pipelines documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Agent Registry now offers public naming capabilities, making it easy to attach verified domain names to your agents and AI tools.
  • Previously, developers had to manually configure how agents discover and connect to one another, which added complexity to building multi-agent systems.
  • According to recent reports, this capability is available at no additional charge at this time in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available.

AWS Agent Registry now offers public naming capabilities, making it easy to attach verified domain names to your agents and AI tools. Developers and network admins can perform domain verification checks to prove domain ownership, then associate the verified domain names with their agents to promote them for public visibility beyond their registry and AWS account.

Previously, developers had to manually configure how agents discover and connect to one another, which added complexity to building multi-agent systems. With this launch, since the public agent records are anchored to a verified domain identity, you can confirm the source of an agent before connecting to it. Once published, agent records are searchable by any AWS-authenticated user using both semantic and lexical search.

According to recent reports, this capability is available at no additional charge at this time in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available. To learn more about naming and public discovery, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation.

#16665. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3316 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Industry observers note that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the upcoming US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Industry observers note that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

In a recent development, reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

Industry observers note that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

It has been revealed that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Sources indicate that attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

In a recent development, the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

According to recent reports, the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Sources indicate that the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

In a recent development, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

According to recent reports, A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Strategy for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

Recent findings suggest that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

According to recent reports, beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

According to recent reports, beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Industry observers note that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

According to recent reports, beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Industry observers note that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

In a recent development, you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

According to recent reports, the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

In a recent development, after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

According to recent reports, training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can enhancement the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the latest weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Sources indicate that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one revision behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Industry observers note that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

It has been revealed that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Sources indicate that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

In a recent development, you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

It has been revealed that our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

In a recent development, we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

It has been revealed that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

Industry observers note that this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

According to recent reports, one question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Sources indicate that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

80% of mid-sized FS firms fear falling behind on AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mid-sized financial services firms are struggling to keep up with larger rivals on AI, with 80% of their leaders saying they are falling behind, according to research from TXP, a digital transformation business focused on tech consulting, development and resourcing.
  • The study points to a squeeze between thin in-house expertise and expensive outside partnerships.
  • The report, titled ‘Partner Dependency: The Hidden Cost of AI Projects’, polled 200 executives shaping AI strategy at mid-market organisations, among them businesses in financial services and insurance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mid-sized financial services firms are struggling to keep up with larger rivals on AI, with 80% of their leaders saying they are falling behind, according to research from TXP, a digital transformation business focused on tech consulting, development and resourcing.

The study points to a squeeze between thin in-house expertise and expensive outside partnerships.

The report, titled ‘Partner Dependency: The Hidden Cost of AI Projects’, polled 200 executives shaping AI strategy at mid-market organisations, among them businesses in financial services and insurance. Its central finding is that weak internal know-how, combined with poor handover of knowledge during projects, is locking firms into long-term reliance on external providers.

According to recent reports, some 65% of mid-market FS leaders remarked inadequate knowledge sharing has left them relying on outside partners to run or extend their AI initiatives. A further 56% admitted their staff cannot properly judge whether systems built by partners are working as intended.

Looking ahead, 77% expect this reliance to leave their own teams unable to oversee AI independently, and 79% fear it raises the likelihood that faults in AI systems will slip past unnoticed or prove impossible to resolve internally before they grow into larger problems.

Financial pressure is another concern. Of those surveyed, 91% believe dependence on partners could push expenses higher over time, while 56% noted spending on implementation partners has exceeded the value AI has delivered so far.

It has been revealed that trust in suppliers also emerged as an glitch. Two-thirds of respondents claimed some partners had overstated their AI capabilities, with firms soon discovering a lack of genuine expertise. In such cases, organisations can face delayed projects or the added expense of hiring a second provider to finish the job.

TXP operates as a digital transformation specialist, offering tech consulting, development and resourcing services.

TXP chief operations officer Tim Hurst stated, “Mid-sized financial services firms often have smaller budgets and fewer internal skills than large enterprises. To keep pace with complex, critical technologies such as AI, partnerships and external support are essential. But without effective knowledge transfer, partner support often becomes partner dependence once the initial delivery phase ends. Costs quickly rise as projects extend beyond implementation into ongoing management. The value of AI is eroded and errors become harder to spot and fix, introducing security and operational risk.”.

Hurst added, “AI shouldn’t be the sole domain of larger, well-funded FS firms, and partners play a key role in levelling the playing field by helping the mid-market realise the benefits of AI. Mid-sized businesses should look for partners with strong security and compliance credentials who can integrate AI with their existing systems. Knowledge transfer and a clear initiative to reduce long-term dependency should be built into every relationship from the start. Partners must build systems that work, and leave clients able to innovate long after they’ve gone.”.
