📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • According to recent reports, A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

According to recent reports, A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

Industry observers note that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Industry observers note that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

In a recent development, A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In a recent development, in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The latest Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

It has been revealed that the decoding kernel indicates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

According to recent reports, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Sources indicate that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

According to recent reports, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Recent findings suggest that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

Recent findings suggest that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

It has been revealed that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

It has been revealed that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Industry observers note that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

In a recent development, pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A massive thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlimit, a worldwide provider of financial infrastructure, has signed up to Visa’s Agentic Ready Program for Acceptance, putting its payment network to the test as AI agents prepare to make purchases on behalf of consumers.

Under the initiative, Unlimit and Visa will examine whether the manufacturer’s systems can handle transactions triggered by AI agents rather than people. The trials will cover how credentials and authentication information are processed securely, full end-to-end testing, and what happens after a purchase, including refunds, chargebacks and reconciliation.

The aim is to confirm that merchants and platforms on Unlimit’s network can accept agent-led payments for their customers while relying on existing card networks and their safeguards.

Visa’s broadened programme unites acquirers, payment service providers, merchants and platforms in an effort to get the wider ecosystem ready for AI-initiated payments on a global scale.

Unlimit operates a proprietary payments network reaching over 180 countries. The manufacturer holds licences across 97 jurisdictions, supports in excess of 1,000 local payment methods, offers payouts in more than 150 currencies and connects directly with domestic payment systems. This blend of international coverage and local integration gives the firm a foundation to serve agentic commerce across varied payment rails, regulatory regimes and shopper habits.

Through its participation, Unlimit is contributing to a shared framework for agentic commerce, one designed to build trust into emerging purchasing experiences while extending the infrastructure that businesses already depend on.

Unlimit CEO of global payments Irene Skrynova said, “AI agents are becoming a upcoming type of customer. They will increasingly search, compare and purchase on behalf of people, fundamentally changing how businesses sell and compete. This will create an entirely new wave of demand, and companies that adapt early will be best positioned to capture it. Our work with Visa is an vital step towards building the infrastructure that will power the next generation of global commerce.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

In a recent development, local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this latest generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

It has been revealed that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Industry observers note that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Recent findings suggest that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Sources indicate that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

According to recent reports, the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

Recent findings suggest that and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Recent findings suggest that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

Latest Update: Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse.
  • Industry observers note that other disciplines test differently.
  • It has been revealed that data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Software Engineer, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

Technical Lead, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Industry observers note that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production.

Industry observers note that other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to.

It has been revealed that data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. It is designed to preserve what the agent reasons over: how tables relate, what business events create which records, where institutional knowledge lives, and how definitions get messy. When those properties hold, an agent's behavior in the tunnel tracks its behavior on production data, even though the two share no sensitive content.

It has been revealed that at Google, we built an internal data simulator to serve as a wind tunnel for our enterprise data agents. Rather than copying proprietary schemas or cataloging every undocumented quirk in a live warehouse, an engineer starts with a short, plain-English description of organizational patterns, for example: "Simulate a two-plant brake manufacturer with an ERP, a shop-floor execution system, and a three-shift schedule where second-shift supervisors track downtime differently from operations and finance." From just a few sentences, the simulator invents a structurally analogous tech giant ("Calder Brakes"), generating its schemas, rows, event history, documents, and chat threads alongside a benchmark of hard questions and a verified answer key.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Production data and its synthetic counterpart share causal structure without sharing sensitive content. A short description of domain patterns seeds the wind tunnel, where the agent is evaluated over read-only tools and behavioral trends carry back to production.

Recent findings suggest that why did we do this? Most data agents are evaluated on small, clean test databases with well-labeled tables, unambiguous metrics, and no conflicting documents. Those datasets are convenient, but they rarely test the judgment that enterprise data demands.

Once generated, a synthetic estate is served through a read-only interface — SQL execution, schema browsing, and document search — that any agent can call without seeing the blueprint or answer key. But consider what happens when an agent is asked either a qualitative onboarding question or a quantitative metric question from our simulated factory, "Calder Brakes Plant 2":.

Qualitative: "A new analyst is joining the team. What should they know about how 'downtime' is handled here, before they start producing reports?".

Industry observers note that A naive agent falls into the same trap on both questions. It searches for the most authoritative document and finds a policy memo from Bob, a second-shift supervisor, which states that downtime means unplanned stoppages only, and planned changeovers don't count. Bob is confident, articulate, and senior, so the agent summarizes his definition — and filters out planned changeovers when writing its SQL query.

Both answers are wrong. In fact, the plant's official metric counts changeovers as planned downtime. Bob sincerely believes his version because it flatters his shift's numbers, but weeks later the metric owner quietly corrects the record in a follow-up thread. Getting either question right requires looking past a document's tone, checking who owns the metric before writing SQL, and tracing later corrections. This is where data agents often fail in production.

A synthetic estate is only useful for evaluation if its answer key is accurate and reproducible. Our simulator achieves this by separating simulated manufacturer’s design from data generation across four stages (Figure 2).

In a recent development, figure 2. One pipeline, one source of truth. In the estate-generation pipeline, only ① Compile blueprint invents facts and ③ Render documents phrases those fixed facts as prose (blue boxes); ② Simulate & build tables (plus SQL answer computation) runs deterministically from the frozen blueprint and seed, before ④ Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Industry observers note that first, the Compile blueprint stage uses a language model to turn the pattern prompt into a frozen blueprint specifying the company's systems, people, metrics, and individual beliefs. Those beliefs can be mistaken on purpose — Bob's flawed definition of downtime is recorded alongside the official metric, planting the trap and its solution together.

Industry observers note that in the estate-generation pipeline, Compile blueprint is the only point where a language model decides what is true. Once the blueprint is frozen, Simulate & build tables runs deterministically without a model: employees act on their schedules, triggering tickets, shift handovers, and database rows, so that every record traces back to the event that created it. Organizational messiness emerges naturally from this timeline, such as outdated procedures or conflicting definitions, while row-level flaws that model real ingestion glitches (e.g., retry-storm duplicate rows, unmerged keys, or a mid-quarter unit change) are injected into the tables. Every flaw is recorded in a machine-readable messiness log so the benchmark generator can adjust the ground-truth SQL queries to account for the messy tables.

Recent findings suggest that given the same blueprint and random seed, the simulator produces identical tables and an identical SQL answer key on every run. The only subsequent step in building the estate that calls a model is Render documents, which turns the facts fixed in the blueprint into memos and chat threads in each person's writing style. Finally, Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Three build-time checks keep the benchmark honest:.

It has been revealed that computed SQL and rubric gold answers: Every quantitative question ships with the SQL query that computes its expected ("gold") answer against the messy tables. Because the messiness log records injected retry duplicates on defect rows, the benchmark generator automatically pairs a defect-count question with the deduplicating COUNT(DISTINCT) query (240) – and runs decoy SQL queries representing common mistakes (like an un-deduplicated COUNT(*) or Bob's changeover filter) to verify that falling for a trap yields a different number. Qualitative questions ship with a rubric grounded in the blueprint's metric owner, official definition, and correction trail. If the estate lacks the data to verify a question, the generator drops the item rather than shipping an unverified question.

Verified documents: Every rendered memo and chat thread is checked against the blueprint to confirm it states its assigned facts without introducing unrecorded numbers, dates, or names.

Hallucination sentinels: The simulator plants questions about invented metrics like "Basalt Velocity Ratio" that appear nowhere in the estate; a reliable agent abstains and reports that no such metric exists.

A wind tunnel does not need to match the exact score an agent gets on production data; it needs to reproduce the same behavioral trends: direction (if longer reasoning chains lower accuracy on real data, they should lower accuracy in the tunnel) and rate (accuracy should degrade at the similar pace as contradictions accumulate). When those trends hold, you can confidently compare agent versions and dial up complexity step by step to find where reasoning breaks down.

We test how closely our simulated estates match reality — and whether evaluation signals carry over — at three levels:.

Industry observers note that our simulator builds on two research threads. In database question answering, benchmarks like BIRD and Spider 2.0 have moved from clean schemas to messy databases, while agent environments like WebArena, tool-use benchmarks like τ-bench, and Generative Agents simulate websites or use language models to role-play human consumers. In contrast, our simulator's employees follow deterministic rules tied to their roles and schedules, so a single seed replays the exact same organizational history every time.

In a recent development, we also adapt an intuition from domain randomization in robotics, where simulations vary surface details like lighting and textures during training while keeping the underlying physics faithful. Applied to data agent evaluation, that means synthesizing every surface name, number, and document from a short pattern description, while keeping the causal structure, cross-document links, and institutional messiness faithful to enterprise reality.

Generating a test estate on demand removes a bottleneck between enterprises that own sensitive data, and the engineering teams building data agents for them. Traditionally, developing and benchmarking an enterprise agent required access to production tables and a hand-labeled question set — the two assets hardest to share across organizational or compliance boundaries. We use this wind tunnel internally to stress-test and harden Google Cloud's data agents against realistic enterprise messiness without touching customer data, and the same blueprint-first architecture can be applied by any engineering team building evaluation suites for their own agents.

Synthetic evaluation still carries two risks: overfitting to the simulator's patterns of messiness, and drift as a live business evolves away from its blueprint. The discipline required is the same one that wind-tunnel engineers practice: Periodically calibrate the tunnel against real-world runs, keep benchmark difficulty aligned with production failure modes, and treat the simulation as a living model. Your agents — and their people — will thank you.

AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider now supports AssumeRole for cross-account secret access

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider now supports AssumeRole (role-chaining), allowing Kubernetes pods to access secrets and parameters across AWS accounts by assuming an IAM role in the account where the secrets are stored.
  • With AssumeRole support, customers managing hundreds of AWS accounts and thousands of services can simplify cross-account secret access.
  • AssumeRole support is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EKS and the AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider are available.

The AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider now supports AssumeRole (role-chaining), allowing Kubernetes pods to access secrets and parameters across AWS accounts by assuming an IAM role in the account where the secrets are stored. Previously, customers reading cross-account secrets needed to add a resource policy to each secret and use a customer-managed KMS key, as the AWS managed key (aws/secretsmanager) cannot be used for cross-account access. Now, teams can name a target role in the SecretProviderClass, and the provider assumes that role to fetch the secrets.

With AssumeRole support, customers managing hundreds of AWS accounts and thousands of services can simplify cross-account secret access. A single trust policy on one target role replaces resource policies on each secret. Secrets encrypted with the AWS managed key (aws/secretsmanager) and SSM parameters become readable across accounts. The target account sees workload-specific session names in CloudTrail events for better attribution. This feature works with both IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) and EKS Pod Identity on initial mount and rotation, and supports failover regions.

AssumeRole support is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EKS and the AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider are available.

To learn more, see the Assume an IAM role to retrieve secrets with the ASCP documentation.

Hebbia sees gains in financial research in tests of GPT‑6 Astra.

Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.

Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.

Recent findings suggest that it could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software manufacturer, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.

In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.

According to recent reports, “Traceability is really vital to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita claims. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”.

It has been revealed that in Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.

Industry observers note that hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.

“When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely important. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says.

A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.

In a recent development, “I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”.

GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.

“In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says.

In a recent development, in Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.

Sources indicate that hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:.

Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.

In a recent development, “Imagine getting an notable signal a few hours before your competitors,” she says. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.”.

Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • National Australia Bank (NAB), the Australian lender operating a nationwide network of more than 700 cash machines, has begun replacing its ATM fleet with a newly introduced generation of Smart ATMs, betting that self-diagnosing hardware can keep cash access dependable for millions of customers.
  • According to recent reports, over 100 of the upgraded machines are being deployed across NAB sites in Australia during 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

National Australia Bank (NAB), the Australian lender operating a nationwide network of more than 700 cash machines, has begun replacing its ATM fleet with a newly introduced generation of Smart ATMs, betting that self-diagnosing hardware can keep cash access dependable for millions of customers.

According to recent reports, over 100 of the upgraded machines are being deployed across NAB sites in Australia during 2026. So far, 67 units are already operating at branches including Liverpool in New South Wales, 330 Collins Street in Victoria, Morayfield in Queensland, Adelaide in South Australia and Bunbury in Western Australia.

These installations represent the opening phase of a two-year initiative to modernise the bank’s entire ATM estate.

It has been revealed that the machines are supplied by Diebold Nixdorf, a global banking technology company. Each unit pairs advanced diagnostic tools and automatic recovery capabilities with quicker transaction processing, with the aim of reducing downtime and ensuring services remain accessible when customers rely on them.

According to NAB, initial reactions from users have been encouraging, with customers pointing to better availability, fewer faults and speedier transactions.

The bank prepares to roll out further software updates over time, adding fresh accessibility features and support for more languages.

Sources indicate that NAB’s ATM network handles upwards of 500,000 transactions each week, a figure the bank claims underlines how many Australians still depend on physical money. Note: the press release does not include a broader description of NAB’s business beyond its ATM network.

NAB executive retail banking Paul Carter remarked, “Whether it’s a small business depositing the day’s takings, someone withdrawing cash for the weekend, or grandparents slipping a note into a birthday card, cash is still part of everyday life for many Australians.”.

Industry observers note that NAB customer Tahan Lew-Fatt, a mother of two, explained that her family uses cash to help their children learn about money. Lew-Fatt mentioned, “Our kids earn pocket money through chores and recycling cans, so they can physically see what they’ve earned and understand what it’s worth.”.

According to recent reports, she added, “If they want to buy something, we help them save and budget for it, then let them make the purchase themselves. We want them to understand from a young age that things don’t just magically appear when Mum or Dad taps a card or phone.”.

Carter pointed to reliability as one of the leading advantages of the upgraded fleet. NAB executive retail banking Paul Carter said, “There’s nothing more frustrating than turning up to an ATM only to find it’s out of service. That’s why we’re investing in the next generation of ATM technology.

“These new Smart ATMs can detect and resolve many complications before they cause an outage, helping keep them up and running when customers need them and giving us the technology to introduce new features in the future.”.

#16644. Combatting adversarial distillation

Combatting adversarial distillation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
  • Industry observers note that as frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly crucial role in how they can be used responsibly.
  • We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

Industry observers note that as frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly crucial role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

Industry observers note that we place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.

Industry observers note that the concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

Industry observers note that our models help owners with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.

According to recent reports, in this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to owners—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.

Sources indicate that we started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.1.

Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.

Sources indicate that our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards.

Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.

We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.

According to recent reports, tool-call coverage is key because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.

It has been revealed that with GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As upcoming messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it⁠(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.

When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.

This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.

Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

Industry observers note that to measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.

We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.

GPT‑6 Astra defender with original safeguards.

GPT‑6.2 Astra defender with updated safeguards.

Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request.

Extracting protected reasoning from the current request.

Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.

Sources indicate that we have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.

According to recent reports, in order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.

It has been revealed that adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed⁠(opens in a latest window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.

In a recent development, we support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.

According to recent reports, supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:.

Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.

Recent findings suggest that keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.

Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

We have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum⁠(opens in a new window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.

As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

It has been revealed that related work from Anthropic⁠(opens in a fresh window) reported a similar advantage when training on full reasoning transcripts rather than summaries on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering benchmark. Our result shows this advantage extends to frontier cybersecurity.

  • The capital comes with guarantee backing from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC).
  • Industry observers note that it is channelled through two established schemes: the ADB’s Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program and the IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TBC Georgia, a leading Georgian financial institution and member of the London-listed TBC Bank Group, has raised $51m from international commercial banks to widen the availability of trade finance for businesses across Georgia.

The capital comes with guarantee backing from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Industry observers note that it is channelled through two established schemes: the ADB’s Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program and the IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program. Because both institutions stand behind the facility, commercial lenders can extend capital to the Georgian market with added assurance.

According to recent reports, the resources are aimed at accelerating growth in Georgia’s retail trade sector. Local companies will find it easier to obtain trade finance, which should strengthen their footing as they compete abroad. Firms will be better placed to run their export and import activity efficiently, and to scale operations without increasing their risk exposure.

According to recent reports, for TBC Georgia, the agreement deepens its existing relationships with international development lenders and builds on its client base in this area. The bank says more than 1,000 companies already rely on it for trade finance services, and it views this deal as a further step in reinforcing its leading position in the segment.

TBC Georgia ranks among the country’s foremost financial institutions and operates as part of TBC Bank Group, whose shares are listed in London. The bank offers trade finance and factoring services to Georgian businesses, among other products.

TBC Georgia director of trade finance and factoring Tamar Khizanishvili remarked, “Trade finance is an important tool for business growth and international expansion. Our goal is to make it easier for companies to benefit from these opportunities and support their development, and we are pleased to be partnering with international financial institutions to that end.

“The secured resources expand the financing opportunities available to businesses and enable us to respond more effectively to the diverse needs of the private sector. We are proud that more than 1,000 companies have placed their trust in TBC, with this agreement marking another step towards cementing our market leading position in this segment.”.

How insured.io is transforming the customer experience for carriers

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Founded in 2011, insured.io was created by a team that came from the California MGA market, where they saw first-hand how far the insurance customer experience lagged behind expectations, and where high levels of transient customers meant people were regularly interacting with insurance systems that often felt complicated, dated, and stale.

According to recent reports, according to Steve Johnson, Founder and Chief Product Officer at insured.io, that experience stayed with the founders as the company evolved. After several years of building custom software for insurers, they decided in 2019 to launch a complete customer experience platform that carriers could deploy promptly and easily configure around their needs.

For Johnson, the idea was straightforward – he wanted to give insurers a way to deliver a better customer experience without having to spend years designing and building it themselves, something that could be particularly valuable for mid-sized carriers that didn’t have the technical resources of the largest players.

In a recent development, insured.io is a complete customer experience platform for insurance carriers. Johnson defines their raison d’etre simply; any digital channel, that a policyholder may need to interact with their insurance carrier, can be deployed as part of a single, integrated solution. This includes a policyholder portal, IVR, text messaging (both inbound and outbound), and conversational AI claims first notice of loss.

According to recent reports, johnson claims, “When a policyholder chooses a digital path to access their carrier online, it’s part of our platform. Our platform is designed to be scalable and configurable for any size of insurance carrier and any line of business, and our core tenet is future-proofing your customer experience, where customer expectations consistently outpace the technology that insurance carriers are able to implement.”.

He adds that insured.io has developed a platform that evolves over time, in order to continuously meet and exceed the expectations of policyholders without having to undergo constant waves of latest digital transformations.

Being able to set yourself apart from others in the modern InsurTech industry is critical. For insured.io, the watchword here comes around being insurance-first.

Industry observers note that johnson explained, “I was an underwriter before I was in tech. Our entire executive team has come from the carrier side, so our platform is built with that mindset: we make technology that works for insurance, instead of making insurance work with our technology.”.

What the insured.io founder makes clear is that the tech giant isn’t a ‘generic, repurposed, no-code platform’ that they decided could work for insurance.

“We’ve constructed everything from the ground-up specifically for this industry, and built for consistency across all channels,” he continued. “While your payment processor may give you a payment portal and a telecom vendor may handle your text messaging, we’re a truly omnichannel, vertical SaaS platform; through a singular integration with a policy management system, we can deploy all of these channels, so they’re all interconnected.”.

Additionally, the insured.io platform puts speed-to-market as a central plank, and Johnson believes this is something that has been lacking in the insurance market for a long time.

It has been revealed that he remarked, “When it comes to implementing projects, especially with customer experience in mind, speed-tomarket is paramount because you don’t want to get caught in an infinite development process, where by the time you launch, whatever you’ve done is now out of date. Our goal is to always get introduced within 90 days.”.

A stumbling block for some firms in the InsurTech market has been mistaking digitisation for better CX.

In the view of Johnson, digitisation is a piece of the puzzle, but it isn’t the whole package.

“Customer experience is truly its own discipline, and it has its own unique solutions outside of the scope of just digitisation ,’ he mentioned. “The sole act of digital transformation is not necessarily solving for CX. While solving insurance inefficiency can lead to better CX, you must take a targeted approach when it comes to today’s policyholders.”.

Johnson believes that on this matter, it takes a focus on CX to improve it, and it’s not just a side effect of improving components within the insurance ecosystem.

In a recent development, A key question posed to Johnson is whether insurers are optimising for efficiency at the expense of experience. Does he believe this?

“I think this is true, but it’s not necessarily on purpose,” he mentioned. “It comes from a lack of understanding about what a good user experience for policyholders is. What may be the most efficient internally isn’t necessarily the solution to keep your policyholders satisfied.

“Implementing a chatbot, for example, can be a great example of embracing technology at the expense of the user experience.” mentioned Johnson. “A chatbot should not just be a feather in your technological cap, it must solve real problems for real customers. Otherwise, your new efficiency might inadvertently cost you customers and time.”.

All of these things combined together, Johnson remarks, show how key it is to target customer experience the right way.

According to recent reports, on the question of whether claims experience is still the defining chapter in the insurance CX, Johnson is succinct, “You don’t get your Yelp reviews from the quality of your underwriting or your actuarial skills. They come from how good or bad the claims process is.”.

Johnson added that insurers are much less likely to get a positive review for a good claims experience than they are to get a negative review for a poor one. This, he states, means focusing on improving the claims experience is a huge piece of the puzzle.

In a recent development, he remarked, “One thing that is crucial for this is realtime claim status. Some 30% of calls coming into a claims department are just to see what is going on with their claim, and that’s because many insurance carriers lack the key piece of the claims puzzle, which is claim status tracking – what we call the pizza tracker of claims.”.

When you’re able to see where your pizza is from the moment it goes in the oven to the moment it arrives at your doorstep, insurance has no excuse. Claimants often have no idea what an adjuster is doing at any given time, which causes frustration and increases call volume.

A key question facing the InsurTech industry right now is what happens when customer expectations outpace insurance infrastructure.

Johnson believes this has been a problem since the time the ‘very first insurance policy was ever written’.

He explains, “Customer expectations will always outpace insurance infrastructure. Insurance has been notoriously slow to adopt new technologies than other verticals. It’s a regulated industry, so it’s certainly easier to implement new technology when you’re selling pizzas than when you’re selling insurance policies.”.

In a recent development, johnson states his belief that this will always cause challenges internally. Such issues, he believes, come up around build vs buy, vendor sprawl, and the need to constantly play catch up with customer expectations. All of these issues run alongside the crucial need of still providing high-quality insurance products.

In a recent development, johnson concluded, “One of the mistakes that is often made is insurance executives trying to design customer experience. It’s never a good idea to design these things by committee, because a focus is on loss ratios, reducing claims, and making sure you collect as much premium as possible may not always align with building a great customer experience. Ultimately, this is why it’s all about finding the right customer facing solutions that can effectively marry all of these concepts together, making the insurance process painless for the consumer from end-to-end.”.

Breaking: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • It has been revealed that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • In a recent development, TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

It has been revealed that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

In a recent development, TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

In a recent development, the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

In a recent development, until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a fresh backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Industry observers note that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

In a recent development, the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

According to recent reports, TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too substantial for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Industry observers note that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

It has been revealed that decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

According to recent reports, we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an matter on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel aims. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

In a recent development, we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an concern and tell us about it.
