Latest Update: Drowning in clicks: Scaling Black Friday pipelines with Managed Airflow agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • Industry observers note that when an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sr. Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Industry observers note that when an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix. It's finding out what to fix. A task dies without a traceback. Is it the code, the data, or the environment? Hard to say, as clues are scattered across task logs, scheduler logs, and worker metrics. And once you know what the problem is, the question becomes whether to add memory, rewrite the DAG, or finally take on the major version upgrade you've been putting off. Answering these questions takes time and deep Airflow expertise, usually while you're on call in the middle of an incident.

According to recent reports, AI agents can increasingly do much of this legwork. Managed Service for Apache Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) now offers agentic help across a pipeline's entire lifecycle. In the Google Cloud console, Managed Airflow Agent investigates failed tasks, recommends improvements to your environment, and checks whether your DAGs are ready for a newer Airflow version. In your IDE or coding agent, Data Agent Kit writes, migrates, and deploys DAGs. In this post, we take you on a tour of these features through a story of a fictional company, Cymbal Shops.

Amira is a data engineer at Cymbal Shops, an online retailer running cymbal-prod, a production Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environment whose workers have 2 vCPUs, 4 GB of memory, and that autoscale between 1 and 6. Every click, search, and add-to-cart on Cymbal's website and mobile app goes to a Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Storage subscription writes the events as newline-delimited JSON files into hourly folders under gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/. It writes files in parallel and starts new ones every 5 minutes or every 128 MB, whichever comes first.

Analysts, meanwhile, want these events in BigQuery, cleaned and with personal data hashed — and they want them fast. Ideally, each file would be processed the moment it lands. But Cymbal's Airflow environment runs Airflow 2.11.1, and Airflow 2 has no native way to start a DAG run when something happens outside Airflow. You can get close: Schedule a DAG every few minutes and let a sensor wait for new files, or build an extra service that triggers runs through the Airflow REST API. However, the team doesn't want all those moving parts, so they settle for the next best thing: an hourly batch.

According to recent reports, amira writes her DAGs with an agent. She works in Antigravity with the Data Agent Kit plugin, which adds Google Data Cloud skills and tools to the agent, and she uses Gemini as her model. Setup takes a few minutes: She installs the plugin, signs in with her Google account, and selects her project and region.

In the agent panel, she describes what she needs with this prompt:.

Industry observers note that "Write a DAG named clickstream_hourly for the Managed Airflow environment cymbal-prod in us-central1. Every hour, load the previous hour of clickstream events into the BigQuery table clickstream.events. The events are newline-delimited JSON files in gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/YYYY-MM-DD/HH/. Transform them with pandas: read each file into a DataFrame with the nested context object kept as a JSON string, combine the files with pd.concat, then drop malformed records, deduplicate on event_id (Pub/Sub delivers at least once), and hash user_email and ip_address. Re-running an hour must not create duplicates. If a run fails, email data-oncall@example.com. Validate the DAG and deploy it.".

Data Agent Kit inspects the target Managed Airflow environment in Antigravity, generates an Airflow 2.11-compatible DAG, and deploys it.

The agent checks the target environment before it writes any code. Because cymbal-prod runs Airflow 2.11.1, the agent produces the code aligned to that version. It then deploys the DAG to cymbal-prod and confirms that Airflow loads it without errors.

Amira reviews the code, and the DAG goes live in early August. It's good code: readable, idempotent, and correct for Airflow 2.11. A busy hour sees about 200 files and 350 MB, and the task peaks below 2 GB — well under the 4 GB worker limit.

Look at how the task builds its input, though. It lists every file in the hour's folder, reads each one into a DataFrame, and then pd.concat combines them into a single DataFrame. The unit of work is a clock hour, so the task needs more memory as traffic grows. That's fine until traffic changes...

The hourly task loads every JSON file from the previous hour into memory and combines them into a single DataFrame with pd.concat.

According to recent reports, late October brings two changes in the same week. Cymbal debuts its "Fall Into Savings" campaign, and a upcoming mobile app release adds much more detailed event tracking. Events from the new app version are about three times larger than their predecessors, and the campaign brings more traffic on top, so an hour of clicks grows from about 350 MB to about 1.4 GB. Holding a whole hour in pandas takes several times its raw size, so load_previous_hour_clickstream now needs more memory than a worker’s allotted 4 GB. Autoscaling doesn't help here: It adds workers when tasks queue up, but each task still runs on a single worker and can't use more memory than that worker has.

It has been revealed that on October 23, the 14:00 UTC run of clickstream_hourly fails. All three attempts die the same way, with no error in the task log.

Amira opens cymbal-prod in the console, where Managed Airflow Agent is built in. It diagnoses the problem and recommends a fix; Amira decides what to change.

She goes to the DAGs tab, selects clickstream_hourly, and opens Run history. Next to the failed 14:00 run there's an Investigate button with a sparkle icon. She clicks it, and a short ‘Investigate DAG run failure’ dialog asks her to confirm her choice. The Ask agent panel then opens next to the page, and the agent starts investigating.

Managed Airflow Agent investigates the failed run in the console, correlates worker memory metrics with task retries, and recommends fixes.

At the end of the report, the agent recommends three fixes: load the files straight into BigQuery, process them in batches, or give the workers more memory.

Look at what the agent delivers! Every conclusion includes the evidence that led to it, so Amira can check the reasoning herself.

It has been revealed that two of the recommendations are code changes, and code changes take time to write and test. With every hourly run now failing, Amira needs the quick fix first: more memory for the workers. But how much? The right number depends on the whole environment, not on one task. So she asks the agent in the same panel:.

"clickstream_hourly runs out of memory on 4 GB workers. Analyze the cymbal-prod environment and recommend how much worker memory it needs, along with any other improvements.".

Managed Airflow Agent analyzes environment-wide telemetry, recommends 8 GB worker memory, and flags resilience and retention gaps.

The agent recommends increasing worker memory from 4 GB to 8 GB, and flags three production-readiness gaps: Database retention is disabled, the environment isn't highly resilient, and it has no scheduled snapshots.

Recent findings suggest that amira acts on the first recommendation right away. The agent is read-only, so she makes the change herself and increases worker memory to 8 GB.

She schedules the other two recommendations for the next change window. With 8 GB workers, the pipeline gets through the rest of the campaign.

Recent findings suggest that but that only buys time. Black Friday traffic is forecast at 8 to 10 times a normal peak hour, and at that volume the hourly batch will need well over 8 GB. The troubleshooting report had already named the real problem: a unit of work that grows with traffic. That brings Amira back to what the team wanted in the first place, which was to process each file as soon as it lands.

Airflow 3 makes that much easier, because it supports event-driven scheduling natively. An asset watcher listens to an external source, such as a Pub/Sub subscription. When new messages arrive, it updates an asset, and any DAG scheduled on that asset starts a run. Under the hood, the watcher still checks the subscription every few seconds, but it does so inside Airflow's triggerer. No DAG needs to be scheduled just so a sensor can wait for files, and no extra service has to trigger runs. Each run gets the new messages in its payload, so it can work on just the files that landed, one task per file, and memory per task depends on file size, not on how busy the hour is.

According to recent reports, A major version upgrade of a production environment isn't something to do blind. Before anyone touches the code, Amira asks the agent in the same panel:.

"Check whether cymbal-prod is ready to upgrade to Airflow 3.".

Managed Airflow Agent can also check upgrade readiness. It checks compatibility of the environment's DAGs with a given version. Amira is checking what problems she might have while migrating to Airflow 3.3.1 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.3). The agent reports the following observations:.

Managed Airflow Agent scans DAGs in cymbal-prod for Airflow 3 compatibility blockers before migration.

Two findings are blockers. The first comes as a surprise: a maintenance DAG that cleans up the Airflow database by hand, which Airflow 3 no longer allows. The agent's fix is to retire it and turn on database retention, the same feature it recommended during the incident. The second, marketing_attribution, still uses execution_date, which Airflow 3 removed. Four DAGs also need schedule_interval renamed to schedule.

In a few minutes, the agent estimated the work to be done. To perform the upgrade, the report suggests using Data Agent Kit's migrations skill.

Rather than upgrading in place, Amira creates a new Airflow 3 environment alongside cymbal-prod to move the DAGs there.

According to recent reports, back in Antigravity, Data Agent Kit's migrations skill takes over. It adapts existing DAGs to the target Airflow version, deploys them, and verifies them. Finally, the agent deploys the DAGs to cymbal-prod-af3 and confirms that they load without errors.

Data Agent Kit's migrations skill refactors the pipeline to Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling and verifies deployment in cymbal-prod-af3.

Two design choices remove the original problem:.

Scheduling moves into the watcher. PubsubPullTrigger is an event trigger, so an AssetWatcher can use it directly. The triggerer checks the subscription every 10 seconds in the background. Each batch of messages becomes an asset event that starts a run, with the messages in its payload. Nothing waits for the top of the hour, and no extra service has to call the Airflow REST API.

Each task processes one file rather than a full hour. Dynamic task mapping gives each new file its own task, and the subscription caps files at 128 MB. A busier hour means more tasks, not bigger ones.

Once the latest DAG proves itself on live traffic, Amira pauses the hourly DAG in cymbal-prod.

Recent findings suggest that success! In a load test that replayed eight times normal peak traffic, clickstream_ingest simply ran more often. Memory per task didn't change.

Before: Airflow 2, hourly batch.

One clock hour: about 350 MB normally, 1.4 GB at campaign peak.

One file, a few MB each (at most 128 MB).

Grows with traffic: about 5 to 6 GB at campaign peak, well over 8 GB forecast for Black Friday.

Industry observers note that each agent works from the right vantage point. The console agent inspects production telemetry with your permissions and doesn't change anything, while the coding agent works in the IDE where code changes get reviewed, tested, and deployed.

Sources indicate that each step sets up the next one. The troubleshooting report offered a wider review, and each recommendation came with actionable advice. The upgrade check ended with next steps for the migrations skill, turning its report into the brief for the migration.

Agents propose and people decide. Amira scaled the workers, ran the infrastructure commands, and reviewed every change.

Recent findings suggest that static inspection estimates the work before live migration. Checking compatibility in the console scoped the effort in minutes, and the migration agent then made and verified the changes in a real environment.

Sources indicate that amira used the agents built into the console and her IDE. Two other capabilities didn't fit her story but are worth knowing about:.

Industry observers note that you can bring your own agent with the Managed Airflow MCP server, now generally available, so any MCP-compatible agent can manage your environments, allowing you to list and trigger DAGs, check run status, and inspect failed task instances. Access is controlled through IAM, and read-only tools are flagged so you can limit agents to them.

Industry observers note that run agentic steps inside your pipelines with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider, which adds model-driven tasks that run side by side with deterministic ones in the same Airflow 3 DAG. Examples include LLM-based branching, agentic retries that tell a transient error from a bad input, and schema drift detection.

Explore Managed Airflow Agent troubleshooting and the overview of agentic capabilities.

Install Google Cloud Data Agent Kit using the documentation, the extension for VS Code, the plugin for coding agents (Antigravity, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI), or the open-source Airflow agent skills.

Learn about Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling.

Connect your agents to the Managed Airflow MCP server.

Build model-driven tasks and agents in DAGs with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports customer managed keys (CMK) in AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for data encryption at rest.
  • Industry observers note that lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for executing user or AI generated code.
  • To get started, create a CMK in AWS KMS and configure its cryptographic properties, metadata, and AWS IAM access permissions.

AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports customer managed keys (CMK) in AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for data encryption at rest. CMK gives you full control over the lifecycle and usage of your KMS keys, helping meet compliance requirements in regulated industries like financial services and healthcare.

Industry observers note that lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for executing user or AI generated code. Use MicroVMs to build applications like AI coding assistants, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners.

To get started, create a CMK in AWS KMS and configure its cryptographic properties, metadata, and AWS IAM access permissions. Then, specify this CMK as a parameter when you create a MicroVM image or run a MicroVM. Lambda uses this CMK to encrypt your MicroVM image, MicroVM image environment variables, and the payload passed to the MicroVM run hook. You can use CMK with Lambda MicroVMs through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or with your preferred Agentic development tools using the Agent Toolkit for AWS.

​​CMK support for MicroVMs is available in the following AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Thailand), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), South America (São Paulo), US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). To learn more about Lambda MicroVMs, visit the AWS Lambda MicroVMs developer guide. For information on pricing for CMK, see AWS KMS pricing.​.

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

Recent findings suggest that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Upcoming Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

Recent findings suggest that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Sources indicate that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

According to recent reports, after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Sources indicate that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

Recent findings suggest that the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

According to recent reports, call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table highlights that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

In a recent development, the table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Industry observers note that each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Sources indicate that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Sources indicate that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

Industry observers note that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table highlights one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Recent findings suggest that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

It has been revealed that key_averages() demonstrates which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

FINRA’s latest outside activities rule rewrites compliance

💡 Key Takeaways
  • US broker-dealers face a significant overhaul of their compliance frameworks as FINRA’s new Rule 3290, covering outside activities requirements, reshapes how firms assess and supervise the business interests and securities dealings their registered representatives pursue beyond their day jobs.
  • The rule takes effect on 25 October 2027.
  • Recent findings suggest that to help firms navigate the transition, RegTech specialist RegEd hosted an in-depth discussion on the new requirements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US broker-dealers face a significant overhaul of their compliance frameworks as FINRA’s new Rule 3290, covering outside activities requirements, reshapes how firms assess and supervise the business interests and securities dealings their registered representatives pursue beyond their day jobs.

The rule takes effect on 25 October 2027. While that may appear comfortably distant, the scale of change involved means firms that delay preparation risk being caught short. Rule 3290 replaces two long-standing provisions, Rule 3270 on outside business activities and Rule 3280 on private securities transactions, consolidating them into a single framework with new terminology and definitions that compliance teams will need to absorb.

Recent findings suggest that to help firms navigate the transition, RegTech specialist RegEd hosted an in-depth discussion on the new requirements. The session unpacked the key terminology and definitions underpinning the rule, along with practical considerations for adapting policies, processes and technology to meet the updated standards.

In a recent development, A central focus was distinctions the rule draws between outside activities, outside securities transactions and transactions involving selling compensation. Understanding where an activity falls within these categories will be critical, as each carries different obligations. Misclassification could expose firms to supervisory gaps and regulatory scrutiny.

In a recent development, the session also examines the broader implications of Rule 3290 across the compliance lifecycle, including disclosure, assessment, approval, supervision and recordkeeping. For many firms, this is likely to mean revisiting how representatives report outside activities, how those disclosures are reviewed and approved, and how ongoing oversight is documented.

Beyond the rulebook itself, RegEd addresses the operational side of implementation. Firms will need to consider updates to written policies, internal workflows, compliance systems and staff training. For organisations still relying on manual or fragmented processes to track outside activities, the fresh rule may serve as a catalyst for investing in more automated, technology-driven oversight.

RegEd also shared insights into how its clients are approaching preparation, offering attendees a view of emerging best practice, and outline how the manufacturer can support firms’ compliance programmes as requirements continue to evolve.

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • Sources indicate that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Industry observers note that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

Sources indicate that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Industry observers note that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

Sources indicate that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

Industry observers note that the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Recent findings suggest that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

It has been revealed that think of a shipping organization that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

It has been revealed that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Industry observers note that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

In a recent development, they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

In a recent development, third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

Industry observers note that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

Recent findings suggest that A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

In a recent development, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Sources indicate that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, amazon Textract Insights brings document understanding to Amazon Textract.
  • How it works: You define the fields you need in a blueprint, a JSON schema that describes each field in natural language, or you can start from a library of AWS public blueprints for common document types such as W-2s, invoices, and bank statements.
  • You can use Amazon Textract Insights through the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI.

According to recent reports, amazon Textract Insights brings document understanding to Amazon Textract. It is a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract, and is now generally available in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights splits, classifies, and extracts structured data from documents in a single asynchronous request. Documents like insurance claims, tax packets, and onboarding packages often arrive as one long scan that holds many documents in no fixed order. Processing them has meant assembling and operating separate steps for text detection, splitting, classification, and extraction. Amazon Textract Insights handles that work in one managed request, with no AI models to train.

How it works: You define the fields you need in a blueprint, a JSON schema that describes each field in natural language, or you can start from a library of AWS public blueprints for common document types such as W-2s, invoices, and bank statements. Amazon Textract Insights can split each file into separate sub-documents, classify each one by matching it to the best-fitting blueprint, and extract your fields. It returns a confidence score for every value and grounds each one to its location on the page, so you can automate high-confidence results and route the rest to human review. It can also return Markdown, HTML, and plain text for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications, generate document summaries and figure captions, and detect and redact personally identifiable information. Amazon Textract Insights reads documents from and writes results to your own Amazon S3 buckets.

You can use Amazon Textract Insights through the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI. To learn more, see the Amazon Textract product page and the Amazon Textract Insights section of the Amazon Textract Developer Guide.

Recent findings suggest that regional Availability: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down.

It has been revealed that the trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real customers and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage firm, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

Sources indicate that in our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:.

Authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

Industry observers note that authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

In a recent development, lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

According to recent reports, an AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the company, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

That is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:.

Recent findings suggest that A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

Recent findings suggest that before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:.

Each person on the team runs one command:.

A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:.

Sources indicate that someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four highlights how.

According to recent reports, that single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need new accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

Gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:.

Recent findings suggest that enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:.

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:.

Industry observers note that partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

OpenAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

Your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

The good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:.

Keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

Industry observers note that removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

It has been revealed that calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

For people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:.

For the app, grant it to the service account:.

It takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

In the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:.

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:.

In a recent development, if your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

In a recent development, the repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

To stop latest keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

Some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:.

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:.

Live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:.

Reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one new version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

Sources indicate that then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

According to recent reports, once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

It has been revealed that standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, new requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

It has been revealed that you can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:.

According to recent reports, know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

It has been revealed that set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

As soon as real users can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

It has been revealed that if your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:.

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

Security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

In a recent development, figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

Recent findings suggest that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

Sources indicate that we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

In a recent development, we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

According to recent reports, what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Industry observers note that in a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly latest solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

It has been revealed that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

Sources indicate that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Recent findings suggest that overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Recent findings suggest that table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

Recent findings suggest that the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

In a recent development, figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Recent findings suggest that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each revision generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

According to recent reports, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

It has been revealed that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

According to recent reports, so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Industry observers note that each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

According to recent reports, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO enhancement.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

It has been revealed that nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

It has been revealed that when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

According to recent reports, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.
